prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

For systems that are severely damaged or can no longer operate normally, reconstruction shall be carried out according to actual needs. 4.3 Urban Furniture 4.3.1 Traffic Management Facilities The color, form, style, and other aspects of traffic management facilities in the same city should be as unified as possible; roads in certain special areas may be designed with appropriate distinctive features. 1. Traffic facility poles: When traffic management facilities such as traffic signal lights, traffic monitoring poles, and traffic sign boards are arranged in the median/side median, they shall be aligned with the centerline of streetlights and other facilities within the median. Where there is no side median or central median, traffic signal lights, traffic monitoring poles, and traffic sign boards shall be arranged within the sidewalk facility zone and shall not occupy or obstruct sidewalk passage or the area adjacent to pedestrian crosswalk lines. Traffic facility poles should, as far as possible, achieve “one pole for multiple uses.” When streetlight poles and sign poles are combined into one pole, full consideration shall be given to the issue of traffic signs being obscured by the light below (“lamp-shadow blindness”), and the relationship among various poles and roadside trees shall be coordinated comprehensively to avoid roadside trees obstructing signs, monitoring devices, and traffic signal lights. 2. Central median guardrails and side median guardrails: Their layout should start from the stop line at intersections and shall not hinder normal vehicle movement. End warning signs shall be set at the starting point, and reflectors, reflective film, etc. shall be installed on the posts. The length and height of each guardrail panel shall take into account functional requirements, manufacturing process, and the requirements of the deployment area. Figure 4.3-1 Example of Central Median Guardrail 3. Pedestrian guardrails shall start from the end position of the sidewalk curb ramp and be laid close to the inner edge line of the curb. For guardrails at locations with fall hazards, the clear spacing of vertical members shall not be greater than 0.11 m, and structures with footholds are not recommended. Pedestrian guardrails that are not fully isolating or serve a warning function may adopt a post-and-chain form. 4. Vehicle-stopping bollards / vehicle-blocking stones: Materials shall be selected according to the location and functional requirements, using durable materials such as stone, cast iron, stainless steel, galvanized steel, or aluminum alloy. The spacing between bollards should be 1.3 m–1.5 m, and the height should be 0.4 m–0.6 m. Reflective film, warning lights, etc. shall be installed. 151 Figure 4.3-2 Example of Vehicle-Stopping Bollards / Vehicle-Blocking Stones 5. Outdoor municipal boxes and decorative covers: These are generally arranged in public facility zones and roadside green belts, and shall not be arranged on intersection sidewalks, at entrances and exits of residential communities and commercial facilities, or in the sight triangle area of intersections, so as not to affect road traffic. The box body shall be safe, reliable, and easy

Paths and paved areas in roadside green spaces shall meet the following requirements: 1. Quality improvement of non-motorized vehicle lane paving In riverside greenways and other leisure spaces, or at locations with a significantly high incidence of traffic accidents involving motor vehicles and non-motorized vehicles, non-motorized vehicle lanes may use colored paving. Isolation facilities may be appropriately arranged to improve the cycling experience for non-motorized vehicles. Figure 1.4-1 Schematic diagram of non-motorized vehicle lane paving 2. Quality improvement of sidewalk paving 11 A. Traffic-function roads The sides of traffic-function roads are mainly non-open interfaces, with relatively few non-traffic activities, and the paved areas mainly serve traffic distribution functions. Paving design shall implement the concepts of safety, health, comfort, and people-oriented design. Figure 1.4-2 Example of paving for traffic-function roads B. Living-service roads The activity groups on living-service roads include residents and workers around the road, as well as people from other areas who come for shopping and strolling. In terms of paving materials, color, texture, and grain, attention shall be paid to people’s perceptions, and localized creative design shall be applied to road entrances to enrich the walking experience. Figure 1.4-3 Example of paving for living-service roads C. Scenic leisure roads According to the characteristics of scenic leisure roads and the behavioral characteristics of the activity groups, the design objective of the paved area is to provide a safe, comfortable slow-traffic environment and leisure space. The paving surface layer shall use natural, aesthetically pleasing, comfortable, and ecological materials, while also meeting the requirement of coordination with the surrounding landscape. 12 Figure 1.4-4 Example of paving for scenic leisure roads D. Historic-style streets and lanes The paving design of historic-style streets and lanes shall continue and reflect cultural charm and local character, and shape distinctive spaces. Road design should focus on creating a historical and cultural atmosphere. The paving materials and texture shall be integrated with the surrounding environment. Figure 1.4-5 Example of paving for historic-style streets and lanes E. Comprehensive roads Comprehensive roads have a relatively high degree of mixing in road functions and interface types. They shall take into account the different needs of multiple characteristics, optimize the slow-traffic travel experience, consider the composite needs of road functions and the businesses on both sides, and create a paving system that is highly adaptable and simple and elegant. Intersections with a high proportion of large vehicles should be equipped with right-turn protection islands to remind non-motor vehicles and pedestrians and prevent motor vehicles turning right from encroaching on the left-turn waiting space of non-motor vehicles, thereby ensuring non-motor vehicle safety. The impact of road greening on driving sight distance shall be checked regularly, and any safety hazards shall be eliminated in a timely manner through pruning branches and leaves or replacing greening species. 3. When setting street trees, full consideration shall be given to their relative relationship with traffic signs, information boards, etc. The spacing between trees in front of traffic signs and information boards may be increased to around 18 m. Where obstruction has already formed in the existing condition, trees shall be pruned according to actual conditions, or the position, style, and height of the signs shall be adjusted. 3.3 Median strips 3.3.1 Design 1. Definition The green partition between carriageways; the one located between the upstream and downstream motor vehicle lanes is the central median; the one located between motor vehicle lanes and non-motorized lanes or between motor vehicle lanes in the same direction is the side median. 2. Layout forms A. Central median a. The central median of urban arterial roads with a design speed higher than 60 km/h shall be densely planted with evergreen plants to avoid glare interference from oncoming traffic at night. 70 b. Within the range of 0.6 m to 1.5 m above the surface of the adjacent motor vehicle roadway, the plants configured shall have dense foliage throughout the year, and their spacing shall not be greater than 5 times the canopy spread. c. The width of the central median shall be 1.5 m or more, and a formal arrangement structure shall be adopted; simple repetition is preferable to create rhythm. At intersections and important nodes, plants shall mainly be low shrubs; planting trees is strictly prohibited to avoid tree trunks causing glare and traffic accidents. Figure 3.3-1 Schematic diagram of central median B. Side median a. Where the width of the side green belt between carriageways is greater than or equal to 1.5 m, trees shall be the main planting type, and trees, shrubs, and groundcover plants should be combined. The canopies of trees on both sides should not overlap above the motor vehicle lanes. b. Where the width of the side green belt between carriageways is less than 1.5 m, shrubs shall be the main planting type, and shrubs and groundcover plants should be combined. 71 Figure 3.3-2 Schematic diagram of central median C.  Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups

- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)

Justice

- Accessibility
Safety

Comfort

- Psychological Comfort

Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.

Urban arterial roads shall be provided with bus-only lanes where the one-way motor vehicle lane count on a road section is 3 lanes or more (including 3 lanes), or the total one-way motor vehicle roadway width is not less than 11 m; where one-way passenger bus volume on the road section exceeds 6,000 persons/peak hour, or bus flow exceeds 150 vehicles/peak hour; and where the average section flow per lane exceeds 500 vehicles/peak hour. 2. Urban arterial roads shall be provided with bus-only lanes where the one-way motor vehicle lane count on a road section is 4 lanes or more (including 4 lanes), and the one-way bus flow on the section exceeds 90 vehicles/peak hour. 3. Urban arterial roads shall be provided with bus-only lanes where the one-way motor vehicle lane count on a road section is 2 lanes, the one-way passenger bus volume exceeds 6,000 persons/peak hour, and bus flow exceeds 150 vehicles/peak hour. 29 4. Bus-only lanes may be paved with colored asphalt. After paving, the lane color is conspicuous and forms a sharp contrast with the adjacent ordinary motor vehicle lane, preventing ordinary motor vehicles from mistakenly entering the lane. Traffic facility poles: When traffic management facilities such as traffic signal lights, traffic monitoring poles, and traffic sign boards are arranged in the median/side median, they shall be aligned with the centerline of streetlights and other facilities within the median. Where there is no side median or central median, traffic signal lights, traffic monitoring poles, and traffic sign boards shall be arranged within the sidewalk facility zone and shall not occupy or obstruct sidewalk passage or the area adjacent to pedestrian crosswalk lines. Traffic facility poles should, as far as possible, achieve “one pole for multiple uses.” When streetlight poles and sign poles are combined into one pole, full consideration shall be given to the issue of traffic signs being obscured by the light below (“lamp-shadow blindness”), and the relationship among various poles and roadside trees shall be coordinated comprehensively to avoid roadside trees obstructing signs, monitoring devices, and traffic signal lights. 2. Central median guardrails and side median guardrails: Their layout should start from the stop line at intersections and shall not hinder normal vehicle movement. End warning signs shall be set at the starting point, and reflectors, reflective film, etc. shall be installed on the posts. The length and height of each guardrail panel shall take into account functional requirements, manufacturing process, and the requirements of the deployment area. Figure 4.3-1 Example of Central Median Guardrail 3. Pedestrian guardrails shall start from the end position of the sidewalk curb ramp and be laid close to the inner edge line of the curb. For guardrails at locations with fall hazards, the clear spacing of vertical members shall not be greater than 0.11 m, and structures with footholds are not recommended. Pedestrian guardrails that are not fully isolating or serve a warning function may adopt a post-and-chain form. 4. Vehicle-stopping bollards / vehicle-blocking stones: Materials shall be selected according to the location and functional requirements, using durable materials such as stone, cast iron, stainless steel, galvanized steel, or aluminum alloy. The spacing between bollards should be 1.3 m–1.5 m, and the height should be 0.4 m–0.6 m. Reflective film, warning lights, etc. shall be installed. 151 Figure 4.3-2 Example of Vehicle-Stopping Bollards / Vehicle-Blocking Stones 5. Outdoor municipal boxes and decorative covers: These are generally arranged in public facility zones and roadside green belts, and shall not be arranged on intersection sidewalks, at entrances and exits of residential communities and commercial facilities, or in the sight triangle area of intersections, so as not to affect road traffic. Paths and paved areas in roadside green spaces shall meet the following requirements: 1. The material and thickness of the paving surface layer shall be coordinated with the road greening style and use function, and integrated with sponge city design. Ecological permeable materials should be used where possible, with anti-slip functions, and polished surface materials shall not be used. 2. Quality improvement of non-motorized vehicle lane paving In riverside greenways and other leisure spaces, or at locations with a significantly high incidence of traffic accidents involving motor vehicles and non-motorized vehicles, non-motorized vehicle lanes may use colored paving. Quality improvement of sidewalk paving 11 A. Traffic-function roads The sides of traffic-function roads are mainly non-open interfaces, with relatively few non-traffic activities, and the paved areas mainly serve traffic distribution functions. Paving design shall implement the concepts of safety, health, comfort, and people-oriented design. Figure 1.4-2 Example of paving for traffic-function roads B. Living-service roads The activity groups on living-service roads include residents and workers around the road, as well as people from other areas who come for shopping and strolling. In terms of paving materials, color, texture, and grain, attention shall be paid to people’s perceptions, and localized creative design shall be applied to road entrances to enrich the walking experience. All-direction cross intersection For intersections surrounded by relatively dense commercial facilities and heavy pedestrian flows, an “all-direction cross intersection” may be used as appropriate. This not only improves pedestrian crossing efficiency, but also prevents interference between pedestrians and motor vehicles. D. Improving the experience of non-motor vehicle crossings Intersections with large non-motor vehicle crossing volumes should be equipped with dedicated non-motor vehicle signal lights. At branch-road intersections with heavy non-motor vehicle traffic, explore moving the non-motor vehicle crossing waiting area in front of the motor vehicle stop line and granting an early green signal priority. Intersections with a high proportion of large vehicles should be equipped with right-turn protection islands to remind non-motor vehicles and pedestrians and prevent motor vehicles turning right from encroaching on the left-turn waiting space of non-motor vehicles, thereby ensuring non-motor vehicle safety. The ground color in right-turn hazard areas should preferably use warning colors such as yellow, red, or orange, and materials may include paint or colored pavement. Where there is substantial mid-block crossing demand, such as along sections adjacent to schools, shopping malls, transit hubs, exhibition halls, nursing homes, etc., and where the spacing between adjacent intersections is relatively large (>500 m), or where there are no other crossing facilities (pedestrian overpasses or underpasses), pedestrian crosswalk markings shall be provided in conjunction with directional signs, and pedestrian signal lights shall be installed as appropriate. B. On road sections with three or more lanes of two-way motor vehicle traffic, or where the peak-hour two-way motor vehicle flow exceeds 750 pcu and the 12-hour flow exceeds 8000 pcu, pedestrian signal lights shall be installed when the peak-hour pedestrian flow crossing the crosswalk exceeds 500 persons. Where the above conditions are not met but the design speed of the road section exceeds 50 km/h, push-button pedestrian signal lights shall be installed. 2. Quality Enhancement A. Pedestrian crosswalks and related facilities shall be arranged as far as possible in accordance with the principle of the shortest pedestrian crossing route. B. No on-street parking bays or bus stops shall be located within 9 m upstream or downstream of a pedestrian crosswalk. In principle, pedestrian crosswalks shall be set at the rear end of bus stops and shall avoid bus stopping areas. C. Definition The green partition between carriageways; the one located between the upstream and downstream motor vehicle lanes is the central median; the one located between motor vehicle lanes and non-motorized lanes or between motor vehicle lanes in the same direction is the side median. 2. Layout forms A. Central median a. The central median of urban arterial roads with a design speed higher than 60 km/h shall be densely planted with evergreen plants to avoid glare interference from oncoming traffic at night. 70 b. Within the range of 0.6 m to 1.5 m above the surface of the adjacent motor vehicle roadway, the plants configured shall have dense foliage throughout the year, and their spacing shall not be greater than 5 times the canopy spread. c. The width of the central median shall be 1.5 m or more, and a formal arrangement structure shall be adopted; simple repetition is preferable to create rhythm. At intersections and important nodes, plants shall mainly be low shrubs; planting trees is strictly prohibited to avoid tree trunks causing glare and traffic accidents.
